item.content:encoded:
After a brief demotion, Greg Weissert has served an important role in the Boston bullpen.
After a historic July that saw the Boston Red Sox use high-leverage arms on a near-nightly basis, one of baseball's best bullpens became injury-ravaged, losing Garrett Whitlock, Tyron Guerrero, and Justin Slaten to fatigue-related injuries. The losses of Whitlock, Slaten, and Guerrero forced interim manager Chad Tracy to turn to other relievers in high-leverage spots. Among those arms is right-hander Greg Weissert, who, after a brief trip to Triple-A Worcester, has come up huge for the bullpen.
In his first 48 appearances of the season, Weissert posted a 3.97 ERA in 45.1 innings pitched. The 31-year-old right-hander struggled in particular when taking over in situations with men already on base, allowing 13 of 29 inherited runners to score, which, at the time, was the third-most among all relievers.
After needing 34 pitches to get through an inning in Boston's 13-inning marathon win over the Chicago White Sox on Aug. 6, Weissert fell victim to the numbers game, getting optioned to Triple-A Worcester on Aug. 7 in favor of a fresher arm. However, it wound up being just a six-day trip as he was recalled on Aug. 13 when the team placed Whitlock on the IL.
In 12 appearances since being recalled, Weissert has more than made up for the losses of Whitlock, who returned on Aug. 29, Guerrero, who is slated to return ahead of Wednesday's game in Texas and Slaten. He's allowed only two earned runs on 11 hits, striking out 13 and walking only four in 10.2 innings of work. Most importantly, Weissert has performed much better when entering 'dirty' innings, allowing only one of seven inherited runners to score.
Despite Whitlock's return and Guerrero's imminent return, Weissert's reemergence as a reliable option will help in the final 11 games of the regular season and the postseason run, as Tracy announced Tuesday that Slaten will not return in 2026 after undergoing a PRP injection in his right elbow to treat degenerative changes in his flexor mass.
Up next for the Sox
After falling 4-2 in Tuesday night's series opener against the Texas Rangers, the Red Sox will look to even up the series in game two of three from Globe Life Field on Wednesday night. Rookie left-hander Jake Bennett (9-7, 3.69 ERA) will get the start for Boston opposite fellow southpaw MacKenzie Gore (8-11, 4.62 ERA) for Texas. First pitch is set for 8:05 p.m. ET.

item.content:encoded:
The 2026 season has been, for the most part, an injury-plagued loss for Crochet, who made his first six starts before getting shut down with left shoulder inflammation that regressed when he made his first attempted comeback in late May.
But the beauty of all this is that Crochet can wash away the sour taste of missing most of the season by getting back as a reliever in time for the most important games.
After that setback at the end of May, it took Crochet three months just to be cleared to throw off the mound again.
Now that he’s been able to do so three times, and is scheduled for a fourth bullpen session at Fenway Park on Tuesday, there is legitimate hope he can be on the roster when the Red Sox open their postseason on Sept. 29 -- likely at Yankee Stadium.
This time, assuming he makes it back, Crochet will be cast in a much different role, but one that can still be impactful.
Figuring you have questions about how and when Crochet fits in, here are some answers.
Can Crochet make it back before the regular season ends?
It’s not impossible. His next key step after graduating from bullpen sessions will be to face hitters. That could happen as soon as this weekend, depending on what the club decides after Tuesday’s session.
Ideally, when it comes to Crochet’s situation, the Triple-A season would go a little longer. But, alas, it ends on Sunday.
It seems more likely Crochet will throw live batting practice and/or some type of simulated game rather than getting into a Minor League game, perhaps doing so multiple times.
Would this leave time for one tune-up before the regular season ends on Sept. 27? Perhaps, but not necessarily.
Would Crochet be thrown right into the fire of the playoffs?
What if there isn’t time for Crochet to pitch in any type of game setting before the Wild Card Series starts? Would the Red Sox still put him on the roster?
Well, if he’s throwing up to his capabilities, the answer is absolutely yes.
“It's Garrett Crochet,” said Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy. “If Garrett Crochet looks like Garrett Crochet and he's healthy and able to go out there and pitch, and it looks like him? Yeah, that helps any team.”
What would Boston’s bullpen cast look like with Crochet in the mix?
In a word, dominant. Through their first 150 games of the season entering Tuesday, Boston’s bullpen has a 3.11 ERA, best in the Majors. That’s without Crochet.
Now, add Crochet and possibly 2024 Tanner Houck, who is on a Minor League rehab assignment in his return from Tommy John surgery, and Tracy’s relief crew could have a succession of pitchers with nasty stuff.
At 38 years old, lefty Aroldis Chapman continues to be a force. He has one of the best eighth-inning setup men in the game in front of him in righty Garrett Whitlock. Tyron Guerrero, the righty with triple-digit heat, is due back in the next couple of days after missing the last couple of weeks with right shoulder inflammation. Power lefty Erik Miller has been tremendous since he was acquired at the Aug. 3 Trade Deadline.
Brayan Bello, who hasn’t had much success has a starter this season but has been largely stellar in relief, is another weapon. Add Crochet and Houck to those five pitchers and the Sox would have bullpen depth that would be the envy of most teams.
How would the Sox use Crochet?
The beauty of Crochet is that he could work out of a hybrid role, meaning he could be available for whichever part of the game Tracy needs him most.
Keep in mind that Crochet was a relief pitcher not just in college at Tennessee, but also for the White Sox before being converted to a starting role in ‘24. He has experience working in the early, middle and late part of games.
Thinking outside the box, the Sox could even deploy Crochet as an opener if the occasion called for it, given his experience starting games.
“He'd have plenty of comfort opening if you wanted to go that route," Tracy said. "He pitched out of the 'pen. So if you need him to come in the middle innings of a game, a two-inning pocket, I'm sure he'd have comfort doing that, too."

item.content:encoded:
ARLINGTON -- Right-handed reliever Justin Slaten’s season is over, Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy announced ahead of Boston’s three-game series opener against the Rangers at Globe Life Field on Tuesday night.
According to Tracy, Slaten met with Dr. Keith Meister, an orthopedist in the Dallas area, and an evaluation revealed “degenerative changes in his flexor mass” in his right elbow.
“Probably just means a chronic thing over time, but I’m speculating there,” Tracy said. “I just know that the conservative course of action is [a platelet-rich plasma injection]. He’s going to rehab and go from there, but because of that, it’s going to probably cost him the season.”
“As we sit here right now, we were operating and moving forward, planning on having to operate without him,” Tracy said. “This maybe adds some finality to the fact that, ‘OK, now the chances of getting him back are slim.’”
The 29-year-old Slaten posted a 4.60 ERA with 39 strikeouts across 31 1/3 innings over 36 appearances for Boston.
“It’s a big loss,” Tracy said. “At least now the finality of knowing we can’t have him back. But you guys have seen the way he can come in and pitch in those big-moment cleanup innings, to get you out of the sixth, seventh inning. We’ve seen him do that, so he’s an important arm. But we have to deal with it and move on.”
Slaten and Garrett Whitlock served as the Sox’s top right-handed setup men when both went down last month. Whitlock returned from the IL on Aug. 29.
When Slaten and Whitlock first went down, Tracy believed he had enough arms to navigate the bullpen. That depth, however, continues to be tested.
Right-hander Tyron Guerrero, who landed on the IL on Sept. 1 with right shoulder inflammation, was expected to be activated Wednesday but experienced muscle cramping in his lower back Tuesday, delaying his return. According to Tracy, the team does not know when Guerrero will be activated.

Wherever Needed, Garrett Whitlock Open to Helping Red Sox in Rotation or Bullpen originally appeared on NESN. Add NESN as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Red Sox have thrived this season thanks to clutch hitting and a reliable pitching staff. The bullpen has also held things down, from Aroldis Chapman closing games to Garrett Whitlock being used wherever needed.
Whitlock has worked as a starter and a reliever throughout his career. He is willing to do whatever it takes to help the Red Sox. That includes another potential crack at the rotation.
Selected by the Red Sox in the Rule 5 Draft in 2020, Whitlock started in relief and has been in and out of the rotation. He has suffered several injuries but that hasn't stopped him from producing.
In 2024, Whitlock posted a 1.96 ERA in four games as a starter. In 2025, he had a 2.25 ERA in 62 appearances in he bullpen.
This season, Whitlock has pitched in 49.2 innings. He appeared on the injured list between May and June and returned from an elbow issue. A spot in the rotation may not be available, but when healthy, he can fill in wherever needed.
"I definitely know my body better and know everything better now, and so it's definitely something I'd be open to. Will I?" Whitlock said via The Boston Globe. "I'm not going to walk into [chief baseball officer Craig Breslow's] office and be like, 'Hey, I'm starting.'
"So it's one of those things where the team would have to be on board with it and just talk through everything and go through it. But it's something I'd always be open to."
Whitlock played in 13 games in July, a month where the Red Sox won 15 straight games. He went 12.1 innings, striking out 10 while owning a 0.73 ERA. After owning an 1.80 ERA in August, he hasn't given up a run in four September appearances, striking out seven batters.
The workhorse's efforts helped propel the Red Sox to the second Wild Card spot with just a few games to go before the playoffs begin.
Whitlock has two club options on his contract. Thriving as a reliever, Whitlock will look at all options, especially if the Red Sox come to him with ideas to improve the team.
"We're pretty good on starting depth," Whitlock said. "If I become a free agent and a team approaches me about it, I'm open to it and see how it goes."

item.content:encoded:
Being the longest-tenured pitcher on the Red Sox staff has been a lonely role for Garrett Whitlock this year, and one he is eager to hand back to its rightful owner.
The right-hander has been elite in his sixth big-league season, all with Boston. Whitlock entered Monday’s off-day with a 1.81 ERA, 31.2 strikeout percentage and 3.8 walk percentage, all career bests, through 51 appearances, with 58 strikeouts and just seven walks in 49 2/3 innings.
On Monday, Whitlock was announced as the Red Sox nominee for Major League Baseball’s prestigious Roberto Clemente Award, “bestowed annually to the player who best represents the game of baseball through extraordinary character, community involvement, philanthropy and positive contributions, both on and off the field.”
But Whitlock has spent most of his excellent campaign without his closest friend on the team: fellow righty Tanner Houck, who spent most of the season down at the club’s Fort Myers, Fla., spring training complex, rehabbing from his August 2025 Tommy John surgery.
Which meant that for the first time in half a decade, Whitlock and Houck celebrated their June birthdays – they each turned 30 on the 11th and 29th, respectively – apart. They typically play card or board games, cribbage and euchre are among their favorites, and get ice cream with their wives.
“We always do something to celebrate, hang out at each other’s apartments or houses, and everything,” Whitlock told the Herald. “So it was weird not having that this year. And so yeah, it’s nice to have my best friend back.”
Houck finally returned to Boston at the start of the last homestand, then began a rehab assignment in the minor leagues. He is on track to rejoin the Red Sox for the tail-end of the regular season, and for what they hope will be the team’s first deep playoff run since 2021, when he and Whitlock were the rookies of the pitching staff.
“So good to have him back,” Whitlock said. “Love seeing him in the locker room, and the guys love having him around. So excited for him to get back with us soon.”
Whitlock is eager to return the title of longest-tenured Red Sox player to Houck when he returns to the active roster. Tuesday marks the six-year anniversary of Houck’s MLB debut. Whitlock arrived several months later via the Rule 5 Draft, and debuted at the start of the 2021 season. Together, the two righties have ridden the highest of highs and lowest of lows in the years since: a stunningly successful 2021 season, their respective season-ending surgeries in 2022, Whitlock’s season-ending elbow surgery in May 2024, and Houck’s last summer. Houck supported Whitlock through the sudden death of his younger brother, Gavrie, in 2023, and celebrated when Whitlock became a father in the summer of 2024.
“It’s huge,” Whitlock said of his relationship with Houck. “Everyone’s left, and we’re still here. … We’ve been through everything together, through all the changes, whether it’s front office changes, coaching staff changes, our health changes, literally everything.
“It’s been one of those things that we’ve been through so much together that just grows your friendship, and so it’s nice to have a familiar face back around, and my best friend on the team, and I’m looking forward to sharing the rest of the year with him.”
The Red Sox plan to use Houck in a relief role, which will put him and Whitlock in the bullpen together for the first time since 2022.
“He’s got elite stuff,” Whitlock said. “You saw when he was the closer in ‘22, how good his stuff is. And so I’m excited for – I think people were writing him off before he had surgery, and I’m excited for people to see Tanner be Tanner again. And I think as soon as he shows that, people will start coming back and loving him again, and it’ll be great to have that.”
Whitlock and Houck are the only active pitchers in the organization who know what it’s like to play a postseason home game at Fenway Park. (Boston’s lone playoff appearance since was last year’s three-game wild card series, all of which played out at Yankee Stadium.)
“It was a crazy ride,” Whitlock recalled of 2021. “The whole thing was surreal, because rookie year, I never even expected to be there. So it was surreal, and loved every second of it, and want some more. We’re ready to get back.”
Though some may scoff at the importance of such experience, many Red Sox players and opponents know that October at Fenway is a whole other animal. Whitlock, and, he hopes, Houck are looking forward to sharing their experience with younger teammates.
“I think the biggest thing I will tell them is, don’t change what’s gotten you here,” Whitlock said. “So many times, people try and do so many different things, in the playoffs and pressure situations, and it’s like, you can’t do that.
“You’ve got to do exactly what brought you to these moments, because it worked. It worked to get you there. It worked to get you to these moments, and so you can’t try and do more. You can’t try and change anything. Keep doing exactly what you’ve been doing, because what got you here is good enough to get you through it.”
But first, the Red Sox must punch their ticket. They entered Monday’s off-day with their magic number down to six.
“Those conversations haven’t really started just quite yet, because it’s like, alright, we still got some work to do to get to the playoffs,” Whitlock said. “Hopefully the closer we get, those will start picking up.
“But I’m excited. We’re at the door, so we just need to finish our job, and get in.”

item.content:encoded:
Now is not the time, of course, what with the Red Sox in a playoff push and all.
But deep down inside, in a maybe-one-day-eventually sort of way, Garrett Whitlock harbors aspirations to try again to be a starting pitcher, to return to the rotation.
Consider it a curiosity.
“I definitely know my body better and know everything better now, and so it’s definitely something I’d be open to. Will I?” Whitlock said. “I’m not going to walk into [chief baseball officer Craig Breslow’s] office and be like, ‘Hey, I’m starting.’ So it’s one of those things where the team would have to be on board with it and just talk through everything and go through it. But it’s something I’d always be open to.”
Whitlock is intrigued enough to have picked the brain in recent months of Griffin Jax, the righthander whom the Rays converted from reliever to starter this season.
Jax, 31, had an 8.00 ERA in 11 relief appearances, moved to the rotation in April, slowly built up his pitch count, and has a 3.59 ERA in 20 starts.
Whitlock and Jax became buddies when they played together for Team USA during the World Baseball Classic in March. They’ve texted about what amounts to an experiment for Jax.
Jax’s take, per Whitlock: Everything he learned in his years as a reliever, several as a high-end reliever, made him a better pitcher, regardless of role. Tweaks to his repertoire, knowing how to attack hitters, and ensuring his body recovers between outings — it all applies to being a starter.
Whitlock has had similar conversations with the Cubs’ Clay Holmes, another Team USA teammate. He made the switch last year.
“We all joke that we’re all failed starters,” Whitlock said of his bullpen brethren.
Take it from the Royals’ Seth Lugo, who beat the Red Sox on Friday.
He and Whitlock have had very similar career arcs: They reached the majors in their mid-20s as non-elite prospects, bounced between the bullpen and rotation based on team need and their performance, and accepted their club wanting them in a relief role. They were excellent at it.
All along, Lugo, a consummate pro and good employee in his years as a Mets reliever, said he wanted to give starting another go — someday. Now, he is in his fourth season and third contract since getting the chance — once he became a free agent — and turning it into a successful and lucrative second act.
“It’s not as daunting as it seems,” Lugo said at Fenway Park over the weekend. “What happens is you first get to the big leagues and you try to be someone that you’re not, just from other influences, other recommendations. But you [learn] how to get guys out [as a reliever].
“Once you make the switch back, you have the confidence. The problems you had earlier in your career, [which] sent you to the ’pen in the first place — you’re aware why those mistakes happened.”
Lugo, like Whitlock, was a late-innings arm. He faced the other team’s best hitters in some of the most important moments of the game.
“Once you have success pitching the seventh, eighth, ninth inning, the first six innings become a lot easier,” he said. “As a reliever, when you’re going into a game, you’re a lot more stressed out than you are as a starter. So you start to recognize what you’re good at, how you can get out of those situations.”
Whitlock, who possesses a 1.81 ERA in 51 relief appearances this year, last made more than a handful of starts in 2023. Since then, he ditched the four-seam fastball to lean even more on his sinker, went with a slider instead of a sweeper, and changed his changeup, which has become highly effective.
In discussing the possibility, Whitlock is a realist: The Sox’ rotation seems full for the foreseeable future.
His contract includes team options for 2027 ($8.25 million) and 2028 ($10.5 million). Those are good deals for an elite reliever — and a really good deal for even a serviceable starter.
“I doubt Boston will do it. We’re pretty good on starting depth,” Whitlock said. “If I become a free agent and a team approaches me about it, I’m open to it and see how it goes.”
Perez on Abreu
Royals icon and Venezuela captain Salvador Perez, witness to Wilyer Abreu’s WBC star turn, is a big fan — and a big believer of Abreu on a big stage. “He’s going to be the MVP if Boston makes it to the World Series,” Perez said. “He’s built for a moment like that.” … Early returns on Adley Rutschman’s cortisone shot last week, intended to alleviate pain in his right elbow, are solid. Against Kansas City, he went 3 for 10 with a double, as many walks as strikeouts (two) — and played three games in a row for the first time since getting hurt. “It definitely helped a lot,” interim manager Chad Tracy said. “You can tell his body language and stuff too, he looks and feels pretty good.” … Garrett Crochet’s bullpen session Tuesday is scheduled for 30 pitches across two simulated innings, a step up from previous shorter sessions.
Tim Healey can be reached at timothy.healey@globe.com. Follow him @timbhealey.

item.content:encoded:
We've reached the "wake me up for the playoffs" portion of the Boston Red Sox season.
The Red Sox have 12 games remaining on their 2026 regular-season schedule. As of Monday, they sit comfortably in the second American League Wild Card spot with a six-game lead. They're 4.5 games behind the New York Yankees in the Wild Card standings, so barring a shocking development, they'll visit the New York Yankees in the Wild Card Series for the second consecutive year.
Which 26 players will the Red Sox bring with them to the Bronx? Who's on the chopping block? Here's our 26-man playoff roster projection with 15 days until Game 1:
MORE RED SOX
Catcher (2): Adley Rutschman, Connor Wong
Cuts: None
The Red Sox could theoretically cut Wong since he'd barely see the field with Rutschman healthy. If Rutschman went down in that scenario, Mickey Gasper could go behind the plate... but that wouldn't be pretty.
Here's the problem with that approach: If Rutschman gets hurt and the Red Sox add a replacement catcher mid-series, Rutschman would be ineligible for the next playoff round. So if he got hurt in the Wild Card Series, he'd be ineligible for the ALDS and eligible to return in the ALCS.
Putting Wong on the playoff roster ensures that if Rutschman goes down, they won't need to add a mid-series replacement with Wong and Gasper already on board. And while Wong isn't exactly Pudge Rodriguez defensively, he's better than Gasper behind the dish.
Infield (7): Willson Contreras, Trevor Story, Caleb Durbin, Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Nick Sogard, Mickey Gasper, Andruw Monasterio
Cuts: Curtis Mead (IL), Anthony Seigler (IL)
Even with Wong on the roster, Gasper's incredible offensive upside shown in August earns him a roster spot as a bench bat. Monasterio is on the bubble, but recent injuries may have cleared his path to a bench role.
It doesn't look like Mead (wrist) will be healthy in time for the start of the postseason.
Outfield (5): Jarren Duran, Wilyer Abreu, Ceddanne Rafaela, Roman Anthony, Jahmai Jones
Cuts: Eli White (IL), Masataka Yoshida (IL), Nate Eaton
The big question mark here is White's health, as the speedster was recently placed on the 10-day injured list with a foot ligament injury. He'll play a key bench role if healthy, but if he isn't, Jones or Eaton are the top candidates for that fifth outfield spot. We're leaning Jones because of his ability to mash left-handers.
Yoshida (hamstring) probably isn't coming back this year.
Starting rotation (3): Sonny Gray, Payton Tolle, Ranger Suarez
Cuts: Patrick Sandoval
Sandoval just hasn't been reliable, so he draws the short straw. Jake Bennett and the returning Garrett Crochet move to the bullpen -- assuming Crochet is healthy enough to give one or two quality innings in relief.
Bullpen (9): Garrett Crochet, Jake Bennett, Brayan Bello, Greg Weissert, Wyatt Olds, Erik Miller, Tyron Guerrero, Garrett Whitlock, Aroldis Chapman
Cuts: Justin Slaten (IL), Tanner Houck (IL), Johan Oviedo (IL), Alec Gamboa, Jovani Moran, Raymond Burgos
If Slaten's elbow is healthy, he's in, but it doesn't currently look like it will be since he was recently shut down from throwing.
Crochet is trending toward being ready just in time for October. So is Houck, but he hasn't pitched in a big-league game since May 2025, and he hasn't looked sharp in his rehab outings. While his upside is intriguing, we'd leave him off the initial playoff roster.
Brayan Bello makes the cut as a bulk arm after excelling in that role throughout the second half.

item.content:encoded:
Payton Tolle starts with immaculate inning, Roman Anthony gets key hit as Red Sox beat Royals 4-1
The host team defeated the visiting club four to one; the starting pitcher opened the game with an immaculate inning
- 1 minuto de lectura'
BOSTON (AP) — Payton Tolle opened the game with an immaculate inning , Roman Anthony hit a go-ahead single and the Boston Red Sox beat the Kansas City Royals 4-1 on Sunday in a game that’s start was delayed by rain.
Tolle is the first Boston pitcher to throw an immaculate inning (three strikeouts on nine pitches) to start a game since Hall of Famer Pedro Martinez did it on May 18, 2002.
Caleb Durbin hit a solo homer and Trevor Story added a game-breaking two-run single for the Red Sox, who took the final two games of the three-game series.
Carter Jensen drove in the Royals’ run with a pinch-hit single. Kansas City was looking for its first series win in Boston since 2017.
In the seventh, Anthony lined an opposite-field single against reliever Connor Thomas after Craig Kimbrel (1-5) walked the first two batters.
Garrett Whitlock (7-1) was credited with the victory. Aroldis Chapman got the final three outs for his 34th save and the 401st of his career.
Tolle, a hard-throwing 23-year-old left-hander, fanned Nick Loftin called, then got Bobby Witt Jr. and Jac Caglianone swinging in the first.
He went six scoreless innings, striking out seven while allowing four singles.
Noah Cameron gave up a run over six sharp innings.
Durbin belted Cameron’s first pitch into the first row of seats above the Green Monster. Story’s single came off Nate Pearson in the eighth.
Jensen’s RBI single inside the first-base bag tied it.
